segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them on ahead of him two by two into every town and place where he himself was about to go.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. So ask the Lord of the harvest to send out workers into his harvest.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Go! Look, I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals, and greet no one on the road.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Stay in that same house, eating and drinking what they provide, for the worker deserves his wages. Do not move around from house to house.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And whatever town you enter where they welcome you, eat what is set before you,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: heal the sick who are there, and say to them, ‘The kingdom of God has come near to you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But whatever town you enter where they do not welcome you, go out into its streets and say,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘Even the dust from your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you. Yet know this: the kingdom of God has come near.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the deeds of power done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever listens to you listens to me, and whoever rejects you rejects me; and whoever rejects me rejects the one who sent me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The seventy-two returned with joy, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, even the demons submit to us in your name!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, I have given you the authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you at all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet do not rejoice in this, that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in the heavens.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very hour he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was your good pleasure.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everything has been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows who the Son is except the Father, or who the Father is except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then, turning to the disciples, he said privately,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For I tell you that many prophets and kings wanted to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just then an expert in the law stood up to test him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is written in the Law? How do you read it?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You have answered correctly. Do this and you will live.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he, wanting to justify himself, said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “And who is my neighbor?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus took up the question and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among bandits, who stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: By chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In the same way a Levite also, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But a Samaritan who was on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him he was moved with compassion.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The next day he took out two denarii, gave them to the innkeeper, and said, ‘Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Which of these three, do you think, became a neighbor to the man who fell among the bandits?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The one who showed him mercy.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go, and you do the same.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they went on their way, he entered a village, and a woman named Martha welcomed him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She had a sister called Mary, who sat down at the feet of Jesus and was listening to his word.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Martha was distracted with much serving. She came up and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her, then, to help me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Lord answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but few things are needed, or only one. For Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her.”

notes.note: The manuscripts are closely divided between "seventy-two" and "seventy," here and in verse 17, and scholars do not agree which is original. The SBLGNT reads seventy-two. Either number may echo the traditional count of the world's nations in Genesis 10, which differs in the same way between the Hebrew and Greek texts.

"Son of" followed by a quality is a Semitic idiom for a person characterised by that quality. Here it means someone who is disposed to peace and ready to receive the messengers' greeting. Many modern translations paraphrase as "a person of peace" or "someone who promotes peace."

The traditional rendering is "repented," which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English "repent" centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct, and sackcloth and ashes were the outward signs of that turning.

The Greek is plural here, unlike the singular in verses 15, 18 and 21. Most translations flatten it to "heaven." The plural reflects a Semitic way of speaking about God's dwelling and is kept where the Greek has it. The image is of a heavenly register of citizens.

Many translations have "I thank you." In the Greek Psalms this verb regularly renders the Hebrew for openly acknowledging and praising God, which is broader than gratitude. Some modern versions also use "praise."

The traditional rendering is "lawyer," which now suggests a courtroom advocate. The man is a specialist in interpreting the Law of Moses, a religious scholar. Several modern translations render it in a similar way.

The adjective is formed from the word for "age." In Jewish usage of the period "eternal life" is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. "Eternal" is the standard rendering and is kept here. A minority of translators prefer "life of the age to come."

Greek has a single word-family where English divides between "righteous/righteousness" and "just/justice/justify." The verb here means to show oneself to be in the right. The man wants to come out of the exchange vindicated, perhaps for having asked a question whose answer he already knew.

The Greek word denotes violent brigands who operate in gangs, not sneak thieves. "Robbers" is the usual modern rendering and is not wrong. "Bandits" better conveys the armed highwaymen for whom the steep, desolate road from Jerusalem down to Jericho was known.

Samaritans and Jews both revered the Law of Moses but worshipped at rival sanctuaries, and they regarded each other with long-standing hostility. In the previous chapter a Samaritan village refuses to receive Jesus. The original hearers would have expected the third traveller, after a priest and a Levite, to be an ordinary Israelite, not a despised outsider.
A denarius was a Roman silver coin, roughly a day's wage for a labourer. Two would probably have covered a stay of some days at an inn, though exact costs are uncertain.

notes.phrase: few things are needed, or only one
notes.note: The manuscripts differ here. Many read simply "but one thing is needed," which most translations follow. Others, including some early witnesses, read "few things are needed, or one," and this is the reading the SBLGNT prints. On the longer reading Jesus may be moving from the meal (a few dishes would do, or even one) to the one thing that matters, which Mary has chosen.

candidates.reason: It ranges across "life," "self" and "soul" throughout the New Testament, and "soul" can import a later body-soul dualism, so a consistent policy is needed.
It recurs in "den of robbers," the men crucified with Jesus, Barabbas and John 10, where translations vary between thief, robber, bandit and insurrectionist.
It recurs in Luke, Matthew and Titus, and needs a consistent rendering that is also distinguished from γραμματεύς ("scribe").
It is a distinctive Gospel verb used of Jesus and of key parable figures, and is rendered variously as "had compassion," "took pity" or "was moved," which hides the links between passages.
The plural, for miracles, is rendered variously as "miracles," "mighty works" and "deeds of power," and should be kept distinct from σημεῖον and τέρας across the New Testament.
